suggestions.rationale: Prospective population evidence supports a temporal association between insomnia and later major depressive disorder. In a population-based cohort restricted to participants without prior major depressive disorder, insomnia symptoms were associated with incident major depressive disorder over eight years of follow-up. This supports focused temporal-association research when a clinically established insomnia disorder clearly precedes a separately diagnosed depressive disorder, but the cohort evidence does not establish individual causation, does not show that every person with insomnia will develop depression, and does not replace a Veteran-specific medical assessment of competing psychiatric, sleep, pain, medication, substance-use, and medical contributors.
evidenceGaps: Sleep or mental-health documentation establishing an independent insomnia diagnosis and its onset
Qualified depressive-disorder diagnosis and chronology relative to insomnia
Longitudinal records describing insomnia severity, persistence, treatment, and depressive course
Assessment of pre-existing psychiatric disorders, sleep apnea, chronic pain, medications, substance use, and other competing causes
Qualified medical or mental-health opinion addressing causation or aggravation in the individual case

sourceReferences.citation: Solelhac G, Imler T, Strippoli MPF, et al. Sleep disturbances and incident risk of major depressive disorder in a population-based cohort. Psychiatry Res. 2024;338:115934. PMID 38833937
sourceReferences.note: Population-based prospective cohort restricted to participants without prior major depressive disorder found insomnia symptoms associated with incident major depressive disorder over eight years (HR 1.437, 95% CI 1.064-1.940). Supports temporal relationship research, not automatic individual causation.

suggestions.rationale: Mapping Expansion Batch ME-11 adds this relationship only as a bounded clinical proposition. Across 14 prospective cohorts involving 395,641 participants, insomnia was associated with increased incident hypertension risk (pooled RR 1.21, 95% CI 1.10-1.33). Treat as population-level association/risk only, not individual causation. Evidence was stronger for difficulty maintaining sleep and early-morning awakening than for sleep-onset difficulty. Preserve obstructive sleep apnea, obesity, age, sex, renal/endocrine disease, medications/substances, sleep duration and other conventional hypertension risks. The cited literature supports only this constrained relationship and does not, by itself, establish an individual medical nexus.
evidenceGaps: Independent documentation of insomnia and hypertension
Documentation satisfying the approved phenotype restriction: independently established insomnia and separately diagnosed hypertension
Chronology and phenotype compatible with the bounded source proposition
Assessment of competing etiologies, shared risk factors, treatment/transplant context, and selection bias where applicable
